parent_catalog.scope_note: The six named identities are research entries in the 152-entry main-branch taxonomy. This file does not assign or alter catalog IDs.

claim_limits: No genre-specific composer route is implemented by this manifest.
Candidate features are research hypotheses and must be scoped by period, region, scene and repertoire.
No exact rhythmic pattern is asserted as canonical for any tradition.
The synthetic analyzer fixtures are not musical reference data and are not evidence of cultural authenticity.
Publicly accessible recordings, transcriptions and scores are not presumed licensed for ingestion, training or commercial use.
shared_research_principles: Represent independent role layers and their full joint cycle rather than flattening all events into one bar.
Treat intentional collisions and intentional rests as valid musical possibilities; only enforce explicitly sourced constraints.
Distinguish a stable reference/ostinato layer from variable lead or improvisatory layers.
Preserve provenance, period boundaries, variants, annotation uncertainty and practitioner disagreement.
Keep identity, structural grammar, performance interpretation, sound rendering and cultural review as separate evidence dimensions.

sources.title: Circles and Time: A Theory of Structural Organization of Rhythm in African Music
sources.scope: A theory of cyclical rhythmic sets, ostinato frameworks and lead variation; use as an analytical lens, not as a universal description of African music.

sources.title: The Rhythmic Imagination
sources.scope: Discusses time-lines, polyrhythm and lead drumming. The concepts must be applied to the specific tradition and evidence.

sources.title: African rhythmics
sources.scope: Describes interwoven cyclical figures and cross-rhythm; not a template for every style or every African region.

sources.title: Gigging on the World Stage: Bossa Nova and Afrobeat after De-reification
sources.scope: Discusses interlocked repetitive guitar parts and the distinction between foundational patterns and improvising lines in Fela-era Afrobeat; scoped to the discussed historical examples.

sources.title: Redefining Ghanaian Highlife Music in Modern Times
sources.scope: Highlights instrument structure and named Ghanaian guitar patterns, while warning that timeline and drum pattern alone can be misleading.

sources.title: Ghanaian Highlife Keyboard Accompanying Patterns: A Performance Considerations
sources.scope: Examines keyboard patterns and their relationship to indigenous drum and guitar patterns; does not imply one universal keyboard arrangement.

sources.title: Palmwine music styles in Ghana
sources.scope: Distinguishes palmwine guitar practices from guitar-band highlife; useful for nearest-neighbour controls and local guitar pattern vocabulary.

sources.title: A diachronic study of change in juju music
sources.scope: Documents Juju as a changing Nigerian popular style; rejects a timeless, fixed recipe.

sources.title: Origin and development of Directing in juju music performance
sources.scope: Describes instrumental, verbal and non-verbal performance direction, including lead guitar, talking drum and ensemble cues.

sources.title: The Genesis of Urban Music in Zaïre
sources.scope: Describes a historical Congolese rumba lineage, guitar/bass/percussion roles, section structure and improvisatory sebene practice.

sources.title: Historicising gqom as a post-kwaito phenomenon
sources.scope: Describes Durban Gqom history and distinguishes its rhythmic emphasis, darker/raw production and slow-burn structure from Kwaito; later variants need separate treatment.

sources.title: Ase trap tse ke pina tsa ko kasi: Sonics After the Struggle: Mapping Amapiano and Black Aesthetics in Post-Apartheid South Africa
sources.scope: Explores Amapiano's post-apartheid cultural and production history and the log drum's role; it is not a complete rhythm transcription or universal production recipe.

profiles.period_scope: The profile must distinguish the Fela-era 1970s/1980s ensemble tradition from later revivals and stylistic descendants.
candidate_discriminators: Several repetitive/interlocking guitar parts can form a stable rhythmic fabric rather than one strummed chord layer.
Foundational ostinato parts may be structurally distinct from more variable or improvising horn and vocal parts.
Long-form vamps and sectional development should be modelled independently from one-bar drum patterns.
research_questions: Which guitar interlocks are shared across the selected repertoire and which are arrangement-specific?
How should horn improvisation and vocal phrases interact with invariant guitar/bass layers?
Which section transitions are stable enough to become obligations rather than inferred from one song?
not_inferred: Do not equate Afrobeat with contemporary Afrobeats.
Do not prescribe one canonical BPM, clave, chord loop, guitar count or horn lineup.
Do not assume every part must avoid coincident attacks.

profiles.region: Ghana; related and evolving West African scenes
profiles.period_scope: Separate early palmwine-linked guitar forms, guitar-band highlife, dance-band highlife and contemporary variants.
candidate_discriminators: Named guitar-pattern idioms and their harmonic compatibility are more diagnostic than a generic backbeat or percussion-only signature.
Guitar-band and dance-band arrangements require different ensemble and orchestration profiles.
Keyboard patterns can function as an auxiliary rhythmic/harmonic layer shaped by guitar and indigenous drum patterns.
research_questions: Which named guitar patterns can be documented with exact, rights-cleared score/audio examples?
How do guitar-pattern variants correlate with chord progressions and melodic phrasing?
Which characteristics distinguish palmwine from guitar-band highlife in held-out recordings?
not_inferred: Do not treat Highlife as one immutable beat or guitar pattern.
Do not assume a keyboard is always present or primary.
Do not infer contemporary identity from timeline or drum pattern alone.

profiles.region: Nigeria; Yoruba and Lagos-associated popular music histories
profiles.period_scope: Must declare historical period, band/artist context and ensemble configuration; Juju is a changing practice.
candidate_discriminators: Ensemble coordination may use instrumental, verbal and non-verbal cues, not only pre-written repeated note patterns.
Lead instruments may direct other parts into dynamics changes, pickups, fills, interludes and endings.
Role relationships and cue-response transitions may be more diagnostic than a static cycle alone.
research_questions: Can cue types be represented as a finite, observable transition vocabulary?
Which direction signals are instrument-specific and which are verbal/non-verbal?
How do band size and production era alter the ensemble interaction contract?
not_inferred: Do not make talking drum the sole leader in every arrangement.
Do not reduce directing to a fixed percussion pattern.
Do not create a timeless Juju recipe from one period or artist.

profiles.region: Democratic Republic of the Congo and wider Central/East African circulation
profiles.period_scope: Declare historical era and relationship to Congolese rumba, soukous, cavacha and later dance variants.
candidate_discriminators: Rhythm guitar and bass can establish the accompaniment fabric while lead guitar supplies interludes and improvisation.
Sebene can act as a structurally meaningful instrumental section with increased lead-guitar freedom.
Guitar role separation, bass motion and sectional transition should be modelled together.
research_questions: How does the rhythm-guitar pattern change between verse/refrain and sebene?
Which bass/rhythm-guitar relationships persist across historical substyles?
How should lead improvisation vary while the dance foundation remains legible?
not_inferred: Do not collapse Congolese rumba and all soukous variants into a single pattern.
Do not assume fixed guitar counts or one sebene duration.
Do not use fast tempo as a sufficient identity criterion.

profiles.region: South Africa; originated in Gauteng and expanded nationally/internationally
profiles.period_scope: Period and production-scene metadata required; distinguish early forms, log-drum-forward developments, vocal/instrumental and contemporary variants.
candidate_discriminators: Log drum can function as a pitched, melodic-rhythmic bass voice with phrase identity, not merely as a kick substitute.
The log-drum line should be evaluated in relation to kick, percussion, keys, vocals and section changes.
Production and low-frequency design form part of the sound, but cannot replace groove/form analysis.
research_questions: What phrase and pitch contours characterize log-drum roles across scoped substyles?
How do log-drum phrases answer, overlap or avoid other bass/kick events?
Which production traits are stable musical identity and which are renderer-specific timbre?
not_inferred: Do not equate Amapiano with presence of a log-drum sample.
Do not assume a universal kick placement, BPM, chord progression or vocal language.
Do not conflate a sound-design profile with a composition grammar.

profiles.region: Durban, South Africa; later scenes and adaptations require separate scope
profiles.period_scope: Distinguish original Durban contexts from later substyles and geographically translated forms such as Afrikaans Gqom.
candidate_discriminators: The rhythmic beat can be foregrounded while harmony and melody remain subordinate.
Sparse arrangements and deliberate negative space may be central; density maximization can destroy identity.
Long-range slow-burn structure and evolving production are relevant alongside local rhythmic repetition.
research_questions: Which negative-space and repetition properties distinguish Gqom from generic techno and Kwaito?
How do slow-burn section transitions work in the selected period/repertoire?
How do Cape/Kaaps and other geographically translated variants preserve, transform or reject earlier features?
not_inferred: Do not define Gqom as generic techno at one BPM.
Do not infer that harmony/melody are absent in every recording.
Do not treat Durban-origin traits as the only valid contemporary form.

future_extensions.note: Research independently; do not use as an alias for Afrobeat.
Needs local scene and practitioner evidence.
